name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
description: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a different network medium than the command and control channel. If the command and control network is a wired Internet connection, the exfiltration may occur, for example, over a WiFi connection, modem, cellular data connection, Bluetooth, or another radio frequency (RF) channel. Adversaries may choose to do this if they have sufficient access or proximity, and the connection might not be secured or defended as well as the primary Internet-connected channel because it is not routed through the same enterprise network.

detection_strategies.name: Detection of Exfiltration Over Alternate Network Interfaces

analytics.name: Analytic 0212
analytics.summary: Execution of file transfer or network access activity through non-primary interfaces (e.g., WiFi, Bluetooth, cellular) by processes not typically associated with such behavior (e.g., rundll32, powershell, regsvr32).

mutable_elements.description: Filter for specific interface categories (e.g., WiFi, Bluetooth, 4G).
Tunable for environment-specific large file access events pre-transfer.
Temporal correlation window for file read followed by network activity.

analytics.name: Analytic 0213
analytics.summary: Use of `rfkill`, `nmcli`, or low-level tools (e.g., `iw`, `hcitool`, `pppd`) to enable alternate interfaces followed by data transfer via non-primary NICs.

mutable_elements.description: Match known interface manipulation utilities or driver invocations.
Tunable to non-default or rarely used interfaces (e.g., wlan1, hci0).

analytics.name: Analytic 0214
analytics.summary: AppleScript or system calls to activate WiFi/Bluetooth interfaces (`networksetup`, `blueutil`), followed by exfiltration via AirDrop, cloud sync, or network socket.

mutable_elements.description: Protocol used for exfil (e.g., AirDrop, mDNS, Apple File Service).
Time period between interface activation and transfer.

name: Exfiltration Over Bluetooth
description: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over Bluetooth rather than the command and control channel. If the command and control network is a wired Internet connection, an adversary may opt to exfiltrate data using a Bluetooth communication channel. Adversaries may choose to do this if they have sufficient access and proximity. Bluetooth connections might not be secured or defended as well as the primary Internet-connected channel because it is not routed through the same enterprise network.

analytics.name: Analytic 1531
analytics.summary: Detection of non-interactive or suspicious processes accessing Bluetooth interfaces and transmitting outbound traffic following file access or staging activity.

mutable_elements.description: Defines how quickly a file access and Bluetooth activity must occur to be correlated.
May focus on Bluetooth-specific interfaces or drivers like 'bthport.sys'.
Tune to trigger only on significant exfiltratable file reads.

analytics.name: Analytic 1532
analytics.summary: Use of hcitool, bluetoothctl, or rfcomm to initialize Bluetooth connection paired with recent file reads by the same user or session.

mutable_elements.description: List of CLI tools to monitor (e.g., hcitool, rfcomm, obexftp).
Amount of time after interface config a file must be accessed to be linked.

analytics.name: Analytic 1533
analytics.summary: Observation of `blueutil`/`networksetup` commands or low-level APIs toggling Bluetooth or initiating transfers, especially if paired with recent large file read activity by non-GUI processes.

mutable_elements.description: Limit to background processes or scripts with no GUI interaction.
Focus on specific sensitive file types (e.g., zip, docx, keychain db).

name: Automated Exfiltration
description: Adversaries may exfiltrate data, such as sensitive documents, through the use of automated processing after being gathered during Collection.(Citation: ESET Gamaredon June 2020) When automated exfiltration is used, other exfiltration techniques likely apply as well to transfer the information out of the network, such as [Exfiltration Over C2 Channel](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1041) and [Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1048).

analytics.name: Analytic 1113
analytics.summary: Detection of automated tools or scripts periodically transmitting data to external destinations using scheduled tasks or background processes.

mutable_elements.description: Used to detect repeated exfil activity over intervals (e.g., every 5 minutes).
Can be tuned to filter known internal or trusted destinations.

analytics.name: Analytic 1114
analytics.summary: Background scripts (e.g., via cron) or daemons transmitting data repeatedly to remote IPs or URLs.

mutable_elements.description: Tunable time range for recurring tasks seen creating outbound connections.
Tunable for scope — service accounts vs user accounts.

analytics.name: Analytic 1115
analytics.summary: Observation of LaunchAgents or LaunchDaemons establishing periodic external connections indicative of automated data transfer.

mutable_elements.description: Frequency of task recurrence linked to external communication.
Port number used for detection filtering.

name: Traffic Duplication
description: Adversaries may leverage traffic mirroring in order to automate data exfiltration over compromised infrastructure. Traffic mirroring is a native feature for some devices, often used for network analysis. For example, devices may be configured to forward network traffic to one or more destinations for analysis by a network analyzer or other monitoring device. (Citation: Cisco Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: Juniper Traffic Mirroring) Adversaries may abuse traffic mirroring to mirror or redirect network traffic through other infrastructure they control. Malicious modifications to network devices to enable traffic redirection may be possible through [ROMMONkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/004) or [Patch System Image](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1601/001).(Citation: US-CERT-TA18-106A)(Citation: Cisco Blog Legacy Device Attacks) Many cloud-based environments also support traffic mirroring. For example, AWS Traffic Mirroring, GCP Packet Mirroring, and Azure vTap allow users to define specified instances to collect traffic from and specified targets to send collected traffic to.(Citation: AWS Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: GCP Packet Mirroring)(Citation: Azure Virtual Network TAP) Adversaries may use traffic duplication in conjunction with [Network Sniffing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1040), [Input Capture](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1056), or [Adversary-in-the-Middle](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557) depending on the goals and objectives of the adversary.

detection_strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Traffic Duplication via Mirroring in IaaS and Network Devices

analytics.name: Analytic 1131
analytics.summary: Configuration changes to virtual TAP/mirror policies that forward traffic to unapproved destinations. Detection correlates management plane API calls with mirrored traffic observation.

log_source_references.name: AWS:VPCFlowLogs
log_source_references.channel: Traffic observed on mirror destination instance

mutable_elements.description: Detect mirror session creation followed by mirrored traffic within X seconds (e.g., 60s)
Define suspicious or external mirror targets (e.g., non-enterprise ranges)
Flag traffic mirror activity by non-privileged or unexpected IAM roles

analytics.name: Analytic 1132
analytics.summary: Unauthorized mirroring sessions initiated on routers/switches (e.g., via `monitor session`, `mirror port`) coupled with outbound traffic from mirrored interface to unexpected destinations.

log_source_references.name: networkdevice:Flow
log_source_references.channel: Traffic from mirrored interface to mirror target IP

mutable_elements.description: Tune based on accepted interface config changes (e.g., audit only mirror session creation)
Define high-risk ports used for exfil (e.g., 4443, 8443, 2055)
Define whether mirroring is expected on edge vs core vs distribution devices

log_sources.name: AWS:VPCFlowLogs
log_sources.channel: Traffic observed on mirror destination instance

log_sources.name: networkdevice:Flow
log_sources.channel: Traffic from mirrored interface to mirror target IP

name: Scheduled Transfer
description: Adversaries may schedule data exfiltration to be performed only at certain times of day or at certain intervals. This could be done to blend traffic patterns with normal activity or availability. When scheduled exfiltration is used, other exfiltration techniques likely apply as well to transfer the information out of the network, such as [Exfiltration Over C2 Channel](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1041) or [Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1048).

detection_strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Scheduled Transfer and Recurrent Exfiltration Patterns

analytics.name: Analytic 1118
analytics.summary: Recurring network exfiltration initiated by scheduled or script-based processes exhibiting time-based regularity and consistent external destinations.

mutable_elements.description: Duration threshold to consider a connection repetitive (e.g., same hour daily)
Known external destinations to exclude (e.g., approved SFTP/backup servers)
Allowlisted job runners or scripts known to schedule legitimate transfers

analytics.name: Analytic 1119
analytics.summary: Detection of cron-based or script-based recurring transfers where the same script, user, or destination reappears at predictable intervals.

mutable_elements.description: Path patterns for shell scripts responsible for scheduled transfers
Minimum repetition frequency (e.g., 24h for daily jobs)
Suspicious or unexpected users launching scheduled transfers

analytics.name: Analytic 1120
analytics.summary: LaunchAgent or launchd recurring jobs initiating data transfer to consistent external IPs or domains with repeat timing signatures.

mutable_elements.description: Regex for job locations like ~/Library/LaunchAgents/
Time-based logic to determine schedule (e.g., ~24h ± 5m)
Transfers originating from non-admin user context

name: Data Transfer Size Limits
description: An adversary may exfiltrate data in fixed size chunks instead of whole files or limit packet sizes below certain thresholds. This approach may be used to avoid triggering network data transfer threshold alerts.

detection_strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Data Transfer Size Limits and Chunked Exfiltration

analytics.name: Analytic 0596
analytics.summary: Adversary uses a process to establish outbound connections that transmit uniform packet sizes at a consistent interval, avoiding threshold-based network alerts.

mutable_elements.description: Minimum repetitive size in bytes to consider as anomalous behavior (e.g., 512B or 1024B)
Timeframe over which repeated, evenly spaced transfers are flagged
Common ports expected to exhibit protocol behavior; outliers flagged if not matching expected usage

analytics.name: Analytic 0597
analytics.summary: Outbound connections from non-network-facing processes repeatedly send similarly sized payloads within uniform time intervals.

mutable_elements.description: Whitelist of typical binaries expected to generate outbound connections (e.g., wget, curl)
Deviation threshold to consider data 'fixed size' (e.g., ±5% size delta)
Number of observed transfers per minute/hour that signals anomalous repetition

analytics.name: Analytic 0598
analytics.summary: Processes on macOS initiate external connections that consistently transmit data in fixed sizes using LaunchAgents or unexpected users.

mutable_elements.description: Agent context in which transfer occurs (e.g., user/privileged)
Used to define what constitutes 'fixed size' chunks
Detect if protocol usage deviates from common apps for given destination

name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
description: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an existing command and control channel. Stolen data is encoded into the normal communications channel using the same protocol as command and control communications.

detection_strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Exfiltration Over C2 Channel

analytics.name: Analytic 0988
analytics.summary: Identifies suspicious outbound traffic volume mismatches from processes that typically do not generate network activity, particularly over C2 protocols like HTTPS, DNS, or custom TCP/UDP ports, following file or data access.

mutable_elements.description: Set threshold for outbound transfer size exceeding typical C2 traffic (e.g., >1MB in <5min).
List of approved processes that may exhibit high outbound traffic (e.g., updates).

analytics.name: Analytic 0989
analytics.summary: Monitors for processes reading sensitive files then immediately initiating unusual outbound connections or bulk transfer sessions over persistent sockets, particularly with encrypted or binary payloads.

mutable_elements.description: Threshold for high-entropy payloads indicative of encoded or encrypted exfil data.
Defines length of time over which transfer size must be aggregated to trigger detection.

analytics.name: Analytic 0990
analytics.summary: Detects unauthorized applications or scripts accessing sensitive data followed by establishing encrypted outbound communication to rare external destinations or with abnormal byte ratios.

mutable_elements.description: Enables defenders to tune legitimate vs. suspicious lineage (e.g., launchd → curl is uncommon).
Focus detection on unusual protocols (e.g., IRC, FTP, DNS over HTTPS).

analytics.name: Analytic 0991
analytics.summary: Detects VMs sending outbound traffic through non-standard services or to unknown destinations. Exfiltration over reverse shells tunneled via VMkernel or custom payloads routed via hostd/vpxa.

log_source_references.name: esxi:vpxa
log_source_references.channel: connection attempts and data transmission logs

mutable_elements.description: Limit detection to sensitive or externally-exposed VMs handling confidential data.
Minimum outbound transfer size before flagging anomalous C2-based exfiltration.
Define expected protocols for outbound data (e.g., disallow FTP/SCP over high ports).

log_sources.name: esxi:vpxa
log_sources.channel: connection attempts and data transmission logs

name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
description: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a different protocol than that of the existing command and control channel. The data may also be sent to an alternate network location from the main command and control server. Alternate protocols include FTP, SMTP, HTTP/S, DNS, SMB, or any other network protocol not being used as the main command and control channel. Adversaries may also opt to encrypt and/or obfuscate these alternate channels. [Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1048) can be done using various common operating system utilities such as [Net](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0039)/SMB or FTP.(Citation: Palo Alto OilRig Oct 2016) On macOS and Linux curl may be used to invoke protocols such as HTTP/S or FTP/S to exfiltrate data from a system.(Citation: 20 macOS Common Tools and Techniques) Many IaaS and SaaS platforms (such as Microsoft Exchange, Microsoft SharePoint, GitHub, and AWS S3) support the direct download of files, emails, source code, and other sensitive information via the web console or [Cloud API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/009).

detection_strategies.name: Behavioral Detection Strategy for Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol

analytics.name: Analytic 0367
analytics.summary: Detects unusual outbound file transfer behavior using protocols like FTP, SMB, SMTP, or DNS, involving non-standard processes, off-hour activity, or uncommonly high volume.

mutable_elements.description: Set threshold for outbound volume (e.g., >50MB in a single connection).
Allow-listed protocols in use for specific machines or users (e.g., FTP allowed for backups).
Define allowed time-of-day windows (e.g., flag after-hours file transfer).
Identify anomalous parent-child process relationships (e.g., `winword.exe` spawning `ftp.exe`).

analytics.name: Analytic 0368
analytics.summary: Detects file exfiltration using tools like curl, scp, or custom binaries over protocols such as FTP, HTTP/S, or DNS tunneling, especially outside baseline user behavior.

mutable_elements.description: Flag unexpected protocols (e.g., HTTP on port 53 or FTP traffic from non-standard tools).
Scope for privilege escalation or service account behavior.
Track movement of file types of interest (e.g., `.csv`, `.sql`, `.key`).

analytics.name: Analytic 0369
analytics.summary: Detects non-native file transfer via curl, Python scripts, or AppleScript using uncommon protocols like FTP, SMTP, or DNS exfiltration through mDNSResponder abuse.

mutable_elements.description: Weight rarely-used protocols in user space.
Track which binaries usually call curl/nc and alert on deviation.

analytics.name: Analytic 0370
analytics.summary: Detects access to cloud APIs or CLI tools to move or sync files from sensitive buckets to external endpoints using protocols like HTTPS or S3 APIs.

mutable_elements.description: Detect unauthorized use of roles for cloud storage manipulation.
Alert on outbound flows to geo-locations not seen in training baseline.

analytics.name: Analytic 0371
analytics.summary: Detects outbound traffic from hostd/vpxa or guest VM interfaces using unauthorized protocols such as FTP, HTTP POST bursts, or long-lived DNS tunnels.

mutable_elements.description: Expected protocols used by VMs attached to host interfaces.
Unexpected network activity from hypervisor processes or monitoring agents.

name: Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
description: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over a symmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel. The data may also be sent to an alternate network location from the main command and control server. Symmetric encryption algorithms are those that use shared or the same keys/secrets on each end of the channel. This requires an exchange or pre-arranged agreement/possession of the value used to encrypt and decrypt data. Network protocols that use asymmetric encryption often utilize symmetric encryption once keys are exchanged, but adversaries may opt to manually share keys and implement symmetric cryptographic algorithms (ex: RC4, AES) vice using mechanisms that are baked into a protocol. This may result in multiple layers of encryption (in protocols that are natively encrypted such as HTTPS) or encryption in protocols that not typically encrypted (such as HTTP or FTP).

detection_strategies.name: Behavioral Detection Strategy for Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol

analytics.name: Analytic 1389
analytics.summary: Detects the execution of non-browser processes establishing outbound encrypted network connections using uncommon symmetric encryption protocols (e.g., AES via PowerShell or custom scripts) to alternate external destinations.

mutable_elements.description: Flag high-entropy payloads sent over unexpected protocols.
Define allowable transfer window (e.g., abnormal traffic outside business hours).
List of known-good binaries for encrypted traffic (e.g., Chrome, Outlook).

analytics.name: Analytic 1390
analytics.summary: Detects command-line utilities or scripts using encryption libraries or symmetric algorithms (e.g., OpenSSL AES, GPG, Python + PyCrypto) in conjunction with outbound file transfers or traffic to external destinations.

log_source_references.name: NSM:Flow
log_source_references.channel: ssl.log (for TLS handshake analysis), dns.log (tunneling indicators)

mutable_elements.description: Threshold for transferred data size or extension type.
Hooks into use of encryption libraries like `libcrypto.so`, `pycrypto`, `gpg`.

analytics.name: Analytic 1391
analytics.summary: Detects symmetric key-based encryption operations (e.g., AES via Python, AppleScript, or OpenSSL) followed by unusual outbound connections from non-browser applications or scripted tools.

mutable_elements.description: Expected outbound connection profiles per app.
Indicators of manual encryption operations (e.g., script strings invoking AES).

analytics.name: Analytic 1392
analytics.summary: Detects unexpected encrypted egress traffic from management services (e.g., hostd) or guest VMs utilizing symmetric encryption without traditional protocols (e.g., FTP with embedded AES ciphertext).

mutable_elements.description: VMs with data sensitivity labels or outside normal behavior.
Expected egress destinations and volume for core services.

log_sources.name: NSM:Flow
log_sources.channel: ssl.log (for TLS handshake analysis), dns.log (tunneling indicators)

name: Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol
description: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an asymmetrically encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel. The data may also be sent to an alternate network location from the main command and control server. Asymmetric encryption algorithms are those that use different keys on each end of the channel. Also known as public-key cryptography, this requires pairs of cryptographic keys that can encrypt/decrypt data from the corresponding key. Each end of the communication channels requires a private key (only in the procession of that entity) and the public key of the other entity. The public keys of each entity are exchanged before encrypted communications begin. Network protocols that use asymmetric encryption (such as HTTPS/TLS/SSL) often utilize symmetric encryption once keys are exchanged. Adversaries may opt to use these encrypted mechanisms that are baked into a protocol.

detection_strategies.name: Detection of Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol

analytics.name: Analytic 1413
analytics.summary: Detects non-browser processes that establish encrypted outbound connections (e.g., TLS/SSL) to unfamiliar or atypical destinations for the host/user, following a data staging or compression event.

mutable_elements.description: Correlates file access, encryption, and network transmission within a timeframe (e.g., 5 minutes).
Blocks or flags untrusted certificate authorities in SSL/TLS handshakes.
Whitelist for known-good applications allowed to use encrypted outbound traffic.

analytics.name: Analytic 1414
analytics.summary: Detects staged file access (e.g., archive or obfuscation), followed by an encrypted outbound connection (TLS/HTTPS) from unusual processes such as curl/wget, Python scripts, or custom binaries.

mutable_elements.description: Restrict outbound connections to non-corporate domains or IPs.
List of extensions considered sensitive or exfil-worthy (e.g., .zip, .db, .xlsx).
Define normal encrypted-traffic-capable binaries.

analytics.name: Analytic 1415
analytics.summary: Detects abnormal encrypted network connections (via TLS/HTTPS) initiated by non-browser binaries, particularly after sensitive file access or compression events.

mutable_elements.description: Trigger detection for large amounts of outbound encrypted data.
Tagging and prioritizing high-value directories/files in detection logic.

analytics.name: Analytic 1416
analytics.summary: Detects unexpected encrypted outbound connections from management components or guest VMs using TLS, particularly after data volume spikes or script-based orchestration from within guest environments.

mutable_elements.description: Expected traffic routes for monitored VMs.
Applications allowed to initiate TLS sessions from hypervisor level.

name: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
description: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an un-encrypted network protocol other than that of the existing command and control channel. The data may also be sent to an alternate network location from the main command and control server.(Citation: copy_cmd_cisco) Adversaries may opt to obfuscate this data, without the use of encryption, within network protocols that are natively unencrypted (such as HTTP, FTP, or DNS). This may include custom or publicly available encoding/compression algorithms (such as base64) as well as embedding data within protocol headers and fields.

detection_strategies.name: Detection of Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol

analytics.name: Analytic 0423
analytics.summary: Detects data access or staging events followed by outbound data flows using unencrypted protocols (e.g., FTP, HTTP) initiated by unexpected processes or to rare destinations.

mutable_elements.description: Set of protocols considered suspicious for outbound data exfiltration (e.g., FTP, HTTP).
Defines what amount of outbound data is considered abnormal for a host/user.
Processes that should not launch FTP/HTTP clients (e.g., winword.exe launching ftp.exe).

analytics.name: Analytic 0424
analytics.summary: Detects file access or compression utilities followed by outbound connections using curl, wget, ftp, or custom binaries communicating over unencrypted protocols.

mutable_elements.description: Flag access to paths known to store sensitive or regulated data.
Define which binaries are allowed to communicate externally using HTTP/FTP.
Correlates process/file/network within a defined time window.

analytics.name: Analytic 0425
analytics.summary: Detects abnormal outbound HTTP/FTP connections by local scripts or binaries outside of standard browser activity, following access to local documents or user data.

mutable_elements.description: Defines allowed automated agents that may transmit HTTP or FTP data (e.g., backup tools).
Terms or patterns indicating structured or sensitive data leaving via HTTP/FTP.

analytics.name: Analytic 0426
analytics.summary: Detects shell-based scripts accessing configuration files or snapshots and transmitting them over unencrypted protocols such as FTP or HTTP to non-management IPs.

mutable_elements.description: Locations of VMX/CFG/SNAPSHOT files that should not be accessed by non-admin shells.
Expected network protocols for guest and host interfaces.

analytics.name: Analytic 0427
analytics.summary: Detects use of unencrypted protocols (e.g., TFTP, FTP, HTTP) to transfer configuration files, routing tables, or logs to untrusted IP addresses, especially using administrative commands like `copy run ftp:`.

mutable_elements.description: Flag commands like `copy`, `archive tar`, or `upload` directed at external hosts.
Define external IP ranges unauthorized to receive router/switch configs.

name: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
description: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data via a physical medium, such as a removable drive. In certain circumstances, such as an air-gapped network compromise, exfiltration could occur via a physical medium or device introduced by a user. Such media could be an external hard drive, USB drive, cellular phone, MP3 player, or other removable storage and processing device. The physical medium or device could be used as the final exfiltration point or to hop between otherwise disconnected systems.

detection_strategies.name: Detection of Data Exfiltration via Removable Media

analytics.name: Analytic 0342
analytics.summary: Detects removable drive insertion followed by unusual file access, compression, or staging activity by unauthorized users or unexpected processes.

mutable_elements.description: Filter on removable (e.g., USB) drives only.
Exclude known, approved backup or sync utilities.
Limit correlation of file access and device mount to a defined window (e.g., <5 minutes).

analytics.name: Analytic 0343
analytics.summary: Detects mounted external devices (via /media or /mnt) followed by large file read or copy operations by shell scripts, unauthorized users, or staging tools (e.g., tar, rsync).

mutable_elements.description: Monitor mount points like /media, /mnt, or /run/media.
Restrict detection to non-root or unexpected users.
Alert on large file access or copy events.

analytics.name: Analytic 0344
analytics.summary: Detects mounting of external volumes followed by high-volume or sensitive file access via Finder, terminal, or third-party apps (e.g., rsync, zip).

mutable_elements.description: Detect suspicious or unrecognized drive labels (e.g., UNTITLED, BACKUP_VOL).
Detect CLI-based copy operations vs. expected GUI usage.
Alert if process and session context are mismatched (e.g., script from screensaver context).

name: Exfiltration over USB
description: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a USB connected physical device. In certain circumstances, such as an air-gapped network compromise, exfiltration could occur via a USB device introduced by a user. The USB device could be used as the final exfiltration point or to hop between otherwise disconnected systems.

analytics.name: Analytic 0616
analytics.summary: Detects USB device insertion followed by high-volume or sensitive file access and staging activity by suspicious processes or accounts.

mutable_elements.description: Match data staging or export paths (e.g., *.docx, *.csv, *.db) to USB volume letters.
Limit to users who do not normally use removable devices (e.g., service accounts).
Correlate events within a short period following USB insert (e.g., 5–10 minutes).

analytics.name: Analytic 0617
analytics.summary: Detects USB block device mount followed by file access in sensitive directories or high-volume copy operations by user-controlled processes.

log_source_references.name: auditd:SYSCALL
log_source_references.channel: Kernel Device Events - USB Block Devices

mutable_elements.description: Look for /media/, /mnt/, /run/media/ paths associated with removable storage.
Detect rsync, cp, tar, zip activity writing to USB mount point.
Define abnormal access patterns (e.g., >100 files in <5 min).

analytics.name: Analytic 0618
analytics.summary: Detects external volume mount with Finder, Terminal, or script-initiated file copy from user profiles, sensitive folders, or cloud storage sync directories to USB.

log_source_references.name: macos:unifiedlog
log_source_references.channel: Volume Mount + Process Trace + File Read

mutable_elements.description: Flag removable volumes with suspicious or default names (e.g., NO NAME, BACKUP_01).
Watch for shell or AppleScript execution tied to USB copy.
Detect repeated or abnormal device mounts during work hours.

log_sources.name: auditd:SYSCALL
log_sources.channel: Kernel Device Events - USB Block Devices

log_sources.name: macos:unifiedlog
log_sources.channel: Volume Mount + Process Trace + File Read

name: Transfer Data to Cloud Account
description: Adversaries may exfiltrate data by transferring the data, including through sharing/syncing and creating backups of cloud environments, to another cloud account they control on the same service. A defender who is monitoring for large transfers to outside the cloud environment through normal file transfers or over command and control channels may not be watching for data transfers to another account within the same cloud provider. Such transfers may utilize existing cloud provider APIs and the internal address space of the cloud provider to blend into normal traffic or avoid data transfers over external network interfaces.(Citation: TLDRSec AWS Attacks) Adversaries may also use cloud-native mechanisms to share victim data with adversary-controlled cloud accounts, such as creating anonymous file sharing links or, in Azure, a shared access signature (SAS) URI.(Citation: Microsoft Azure Storage Shared Access Signature) Incidents have been observed where adversaries have created backups of cloud instances and transferred them to separate accounts.(Citation: DOJ GRU Indictment Jul 2018)

detection_strategies.name: Cross-Platform Detection of Data Transfer to Cloud Account

analytics.name: Analytic 1580
analytics.summary: Detects snapshot sharing, backup exports, or data object transfers from victim-owned cloud accounts to other cloud identities within the same provider (e.g., AWS, Azure) using snapshot sharing, S3 bucket policy updates, or SAS URI generation.

log_source_references.name: AWS:VPCFlowLogs
log_source_references.channel: High volume internal-to-internal IP transfer or cross-account cloud transfer

mutable_elements.description: List of external cloud accounts authorized for snapshot or bucket sharing
Geographic region in which the sharing occurs (may impact logging availability)
Threshold to alert on snapshot size or object volume
Temporal window between snapshot creation and external sharing

analytics.name: Analytic 1581
analytics.summary: Detects user activity that shares or syncs files with external domains via link generation, OneDrive external sharing, or file transfer actions involving non-whitelisted partner tenants.

mutable_elements.description: Known partner or adversarial cloud identities/domains
Duration between file access and external sharing
Type of link (anonymous, internal, organization-wide) to alert on

analytics.name: Analytic 1582
analytics.summary: Detects use of built-in SaaS sharing mechanisms to transfer ownership or share access of critical data to external tenants or untrusted users through API calls or link generation features.

mutable_elements.description: Whether the user is in a high-privileged or VIP group
Allowlist or blocklist of external SaaS domains
Size or number of shared files triggering alert

log_sources.name: AWS:VPCFlowLogs
log_sources.channel: High volume internal-to-internal IP transfer or cross-account cloud transfer

name: Exfiltration Over Web Service
description: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service to exfiltrate data rather than their primary command and control channel. Popular Web services acting as an exfiltration mechanism may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to compromise. Firewall rules may also already exist to permit traffic to these services. Web service providers also commonly use SSL/TLS encryption, giving adversaries an added level of protection.

name: Exfiltration to Text Storage Sites
description: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to text storage sites instead of their primary command and control channel. Text storage sites, such as pastebin[.]com, are commonly used by developers to share code and other information. Text storage sites are often used to host malicious code for C2 communication (e.g., [Stage Capabilities](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1608)), but adversaries may also use these sites to exfiltrate collected data. Furthermore, paid features and encryption options may allow adversaries to conceal and store data more securely.(Citation: Pastebin EchoSec) **Note:** This is distinct from [Exfiltration to Code Repository](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1567/001), which highlight access to code repositories via APIs.

name: Exfiltration Over Webhook
description: Adversaries may exfiltrate data to a webhook endpoint rather than over their primary command and control channel. Webhooks are simple mechanisms for allowing a server to push data over HTTP/S to a client without the need for the client to continuously poll the server.(Citation: RedHat Webhooks) Many public and commercial services, such as Discord, Slack, and `webhook.site`, support the creation of webhook endpoints that can be used by other services, such as Github, Jira, or Trello.(Citation: Discord Intro to Webhooks) When changes happen in the linked services (such as pushing a repository update or modifying a ticket), these services will automatically post the data to the webhook endpoint for use by the consuming application. Adversaries may link an adversary-owned environment to a victim-owned SaaS service to achieve repeated [Automated Exfiltration](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1020) of emails, chat messages, and other data.(Citation: Push Security SaaS Attacks Repository Webhooks) Alternatively, instead of linking the webhook endpoint to a service, an adversary can manually post staged data directly to the URL in order to exfiltrate it.(Citation: Microsoft SQL Server) Access to webhook endpoints is often over HTTPS, which gives the adversary an additional level of protection. Exfiltration leveraging webhooks can also blend in with normal network traffic if the webhook endpoint points to a commonly used SaaS application or collaboration service.(Citation: CyberArk Labs Discord)(Citation: Talos Discord Webhook Abuse)(Citation: Checkmarx Webhooks)

detection_strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Exfiltration Over Webhook
